text: egami holds open-ended answers Experiment 3 Egami et al. (2022). Respondents read 28-year-old man convicted entering United States illegally. treatment condition (treat = 1), previously served two prison sentences, one violent crime, deported. control condition, never imprisoned. text: direction, label_features() ranks training texts score shows language model random texts bottom 10%, middle top 10%. model names top texts others . prompt direction 2. fidelity = TRUE without dry_run, label_features() sends prompts gpt-4.1 checks label training texts labeler see: precision recall measure well label picks direction’s top texts. stored labels returned.
code: prompts <- label_features(d$text[d$train], E[d$train, ], W, dry_run = TRUE) cat(prompts[3]) #> You are a machine learning researcher studying one direction in a text-embedding space. Every text has a score on this direction. #> Below, texts are grouped by their score, from the lowest scores (Group 1) to the highest (Group 3). Each group shows randomly chosen texts from its range. #> Your goal is to describe what the texts with the highest scores (Group 3) do that the other texts do not. Use the lower groups to tell which features of Group 3 are distinctive and which are common to all texts. #>  #> GROUP 1 (score percentiles 0-10; 7 of 53 texts shown): #> - If anything, the person should be deported if they illegally entered the country. The government should work with the mother nation and repatriate the person as best possible. Prison time would not be appropriate for this situation. #> - I think the man should just be sent back to the country of his citizenship, where he came from. I don't think that he should be placed in jail because he was just seeking a better life for himself #> - People entering the country illegally should not be imprisoned, but they should be detained and then sent back to their country of origin. They should be coming here through legal channels. We cannot just accept everyone who illegally makes it across our border. #> - The gentleman should not be sent to prison as this was essentially a victimless crime. Assuming he would be deported, which would be punishment enough. #> - He shouldn't be sent to jail, but rather deported. We shouldn't have to pay to house him and feed him while serving time. He should immediately be deported and if he wants to come to our country he should fill out the proper paperwork and go through the proper channels. #> - No he should not be put in jail. He should just be made to go home and showed how to come here properly next time and be grounded from coming back for like 90 days or something. #> - I don't think it's fair to send the man to prison, he hasn't done enough to warrant that in my opinion. I think they should just send him back to his country. #>  #> GROUP 2 (score percentiles 45-55; 7 of 53 texts shown): #> - This isn't that big of a deal. Just let it go. #> - just based on my gut feeling this is how i feel. I feel he should not be sent to prison . Actions should be avoided for the time being. #> - I don't think entering a country illegally should be seen as a serious crime. His past is a bit sketchy, but that isn't a good reason to send him to prison. #> - He is not violent or a threat to society, but simply immigrated illegally. The U.S. should either deport him and ensure he is safe where he will be or help to set him up to be a productive citizen. #> - I don't think trying to immigrate should be a criminal offense. That's not a criminal to me. A criminal is someone who I wouldn't feel safe around, who needs to be locked up to protect the rest of us. The path to citizenship is already difficult enough. #> - Given how the illegal alien has continuously violated U.S. law, the U.S. government should imprison this individual for life, to send a message that violations of immigration law will not be tolerated. The U.S. government should also consider commuting the illegal alien's sentence to another prison in a different foreign country, as a means of ensuring that the home country doesn't simply let one of its own off the hook once the dust settles down. #> - Coming here illegally isn't a jailable offense. I think he should be deported again. If he comes back and then commits a violent crime, he should be prosecuted for that. #>  #> GROUP 3 (score percentiles 90-100; 7 of 53 texts shown): #> - He has a history of violence, and we have enough of that in America. History with a violent criminal past and time served. #> - The person has a record already, and has been in prison before. This person should be deported. #> - Since he had served two prison sentences each more than a year, he has a bad history of crime. Since we had deported him once before because of a violent crime, I do not think he should be allowed to in the country. #> - I feel that entering the US illegally as well as having committed a violent crime means he poses a threat to any citizen he comes in contact. He is a proven criminal. He deserves to be locked up. #> - Well its not his first time breaking the law and that should be taken into account. He has proven he still has litle respect for rules and needs to be held acceptable. #> - He is a repeat offender with fairly bad crimes so he deserves to be thrown into prison. He was also a violent offender which makes the prison sentence all the more necessary. #> - This individual has had a violent crime on his record, and should not be allowed to stay in this country with that on his record. #>  #> Rules for your label: #> - Describe a concrete, objective feature of the texts (what they say, argue or propose, or how they say it), not an abstract concept. #> - The feature must fit most texts in Group 3, not only one or two of them, and be rarer in the lower groups. Do not describe something that all groups share. #> - Use at most 15 words. #>  #> Example labels from other studies: #> - "praises the taste of the food" #> - "gives specific numbers and dates" #>  #> Answer in exactly this format and nothing else: #> LABEL: "<label>" print(data.frame(feature = 0:6, f1 = round(egami$fidelity$f1, 2),                  label = substr(egami$labels, 1, 70)), right = FALSE) #>   feature f1   label                                                                  #> 1 0       0.60 mentions considering additional circumstances or details before decidi #> 2 1       0.38 mentions following legal procedures or laws as justification for depor #> 3 2       0.93 emphasizes the person's violent or criminal history as justification f #> 4 3       0.20 explicitly states that breaking the law requires imprisonment or punis #> 5 4       0.77 emphasizes avoiding U.S. taxpayer expense by deporting rather than imp #> 6 5       0.29 explicitly argue that prison is too harsh and only deportation is appr #> 7 6       0.68 asks for or considers the immigrant’s personal reasons or circumstance

title: SAE regression: an embedding regression decomposed onto SAE directions — saereg
text: formula E ~ treat + covariates | fe1 + fe2. left side embedding matrix (documents x dimensions), found data formula's environment. Fixed effects | absorbed (fixest::demean()); combine variables beforehand interacted effects (e.g. member x stack). data Data frame variables. Rows missing value dropped. W Decoder directions (dimensions x M), unit-length columns, SAE trained texts used . term Column(s) design whose effect decomposed; default first variable right side. Several terms (e.g. party-specific treatment indicators) estimated jointly decomposed one one. cluster One-sided formula, e.g. ~ member: jackknife bootstrap cluster. Required fixed effects rows. strata One-sided formula, constant within clusters: bootstrap resamples within stratum (e.g. ever-treated never-treated members). test "permutation" "bootstrap". draws Permutations bootstrap draws. seed Permutations: set.seed(seed) , one draw another. Bootstrap: draw b uses set.seed(seed + b), draw can re-run . level Confidence level intervals. activations Optional SAE activations (documents x M, rows E). labels Optional labels M directions. rows Optional row E row data, rows share embedding (e.g. member-day's mean several stacks); weights summed per embedding. cores Cores jackknife bootstrap refits (parallel::mclapply).

title: SAE regression: an embedding regression decomposed onto SAE directions — saereg
text: Overall effect (global, one row per term): norm_sq_raw = ||beta||^2, biased upward sampling noise; norm_sq_cor subtracts noise, sum_k V(beta_k) (Green et al. 2025): HC2 variance without cluster, cluster-jackknife variance . se, ci_lo, ci_hi: jackknife standard error normal interval norm_sq_cor, correction held full-sample value. p: global test beta = 0. test = "permutation" (randomized designs, clusters): Freedman-Lane, residuals model without term permuted, statistic ||beta||^2. test = "bootstrap" (e.g. difference--differences): clusters (documents) resampled within strata, statistic ||beta_b - beta||^2 ||beta||^2. report p = (1 + #draws >= observed) / (draws + 1). Decomposition (features, one row per term x direction w_j): alpha = t(w_j) beta: far texts move towards (> 0) away (< 0) w_j. delta = G^-1 alpha, G = t(W) W: effect along w_j directions held fixed (beta regressed directions). q_j = delta_j alpha_j / ||beta||^2: direction j's share effect; q_j add R^2. q_j_cor subtracts noise, (G^-1 V_alpha)_jj, divides norm_sq_cor. Standard errors, intervals normal p-values leave-one-jackknife: closed form documents without cluster, refits leaving one cluster . activations (SAE's a_ij): gamma, effect activation; on_shift, effect 1(a_ij > 0); share_on, share documents using j. Joint shares (joint): R^2 = t(alpha) G^-1 alpha / ||beta||^2, share effect span directions, raw corrected; two three directions largest q_j_cor (biased upward selection).
